prompt:
*(Power Question 2005: Cantor County.)* In Cantor County the address $h$ of each building is an infinitely long sequence $a_1a_2a_3\ldots$ where each $a_i=0$ or $1$. For example, $h=0110100111011\ldots$ indicates the address of a building. If the address has a repeating block of digits, as in $h=011100110011100\ldots$, we use a bar as for repeating decimals: $h=0111\overline{0011}\ldots$ (the bar marks the repeating block). We assume that all possible addresses are in use, i.e. each string refers to an actual building.

The Cantor Postal Service measures the distance between two buildings with addresses $h_1=a_1a_2a_3\ldots$ and $h_2=b_1b_2b_3\ldots$ as follows. Let $D=\{i: a_i\ne b_i\}$. If $D\neq\varnothing$, the *distance* between $h_1$ and $h_2$, written $d(h_1,h_2)$, equals $2^{-n}$ where $n$ is the smallest element of $D$. If $D=\varnothing$, then $d(h_1,h_2)=0$. The address of the Cantor post office is $000\ldots=\overline0$.

Let $h_1=\overline{110}$ and $h_2=10011110111100\ldots$. Compute $d(h_1,h_2)$.

solutions.title: Find the first difference
solutions.body:
$h_1=110110110\ldots$ and $h_2=1001\ldots$. The first digits agree ($1$), the second digits differ ($1$ vs $0$), so $n=2$ and $d(h_1,h_2)=2^{-2}=\frac14$.

**Answer: $\frac14$**

Georg leaves the Cantor post office, goes to Cantor High School, address $\overline{001}$, and then to the hospital, address $\overline{0011}$. Compute the difference between the length of that trip and the length of the trip from the post office directly to the hospital.

solutions.title: Compute three distances

The address of the Cantor post office is $000\ldots=\overline0$.

Prove that $d$ satisfies the triangle inequality. That is, if $h_1$, $h_2$ and $h_3$ are any three distinct addresses, then $d(h_1,h_2)+d(h_2,h_3)\ge d(h_1,h_3)$.

solutions.title: Look at the first place where $h_1$ and $h_3$ differ
solutions.body: Let $n$ be the first place where $h_1$ and $h_3$ differ, so $d(h_1,h_3)=2^{-n}$. Let $b$ be the $n$-th digit of $h_2$. Since the $n$-th digits of $h_1$ and $h_3$ differ, $b$ differs from at least one of them, say from the $n$-th digit of $h_i$ ($i=1$ or $3$). Then $h_2$ and $h_i$ differ in some place $m\le n$, so $d(h_2,h_i)\ge2^{-n}=d(h_1,h_3)$. Therefore one of the two terms on the left is already at least $d(h_1,h_3)$, and the sum is too. ∎

The address of the Cantor post office is $000\ldots=\overline0$.

Prove that $d$ never satisfies the Pythagorean Theorem. That is, prove there are no distinct addresses $h_1$, $h_2$ and $h_3$ such that $\bigl(d(h_1,h_2)\bigr)^2+\bigl(d(h_2,h_3)\bigr)^2=\bigl(d(h_1,h_3)\bigr)^2$.

solutions.title: Powers of two
solutions.body:
Write $d(h_1,h_2)=2^{-a}$, $d(h_2,h_3)=2^{-b}$, $d(h_1,h_3)=2^{-c}$ with positive integers $a,b,c$ (the addresses are distinct). Suppose $2^{-2a}+2^{-2b}=2^{-2c}$; by symmetry assume $a\ge b$. Multiply by $2^{2a}$:
$$1+2^{2a-2b}=2^{2a-2c}.$$
If $a>b$ the left side is odd and greater than $1$, so it is not a power of $2$, a contradiction. If $a=b$ the left side is $2=2^1$, which would need $2a-2c=1$, impossible because $2a-2c$ is even. ∎

solutions.title: Using the triangle inequality
solutions.body: By Problem 2b, one of $d(h_1,h_2)$, $d(h_2,h_3)$ is at least $d(h_1,h_3)$. Then $d(h_1,h_2)^2+d(h_2,h_3)^2>d(h_1,h_3)^2$ (both squares are positive), so equality is impossible. ∎

solutions.title: Strictly decreasing powers of two

The Cantor Postal Service measures the distance between two buildings with addresses $h_1=a_1a_2a_3\ldots$ and $h_2=b_1b_2b_3\ldots$ as follows. Let $D=\{i: a_i\ne b_i\}$. If $D\neq\varnothing$, the *distance* between $h_1$ and $h_2$, written $d(h_1,h_2)$, equals $2^{-n}$ where $n$ is the smallest element of $D$. If $D=\varnothing$, then $d(h_1,h_2)=0$. The address of the Cantor post office is $000\ldots=\overline0$.

The postal service discovers that all machines from this manufacturer delete a consecutive string of digits of finite length from the beginning of an address. Determine those buildings that would *never* receive their own mail, no matter how many digits are deleted.
answer: Exactly the buildings whose address is not purely periodic (not of the form $\overline{B}$ for a finite block $B$).

solutions.title: Own mail means periodic
solutions.body:
Suppose the machine deletes the first $k\ge1$ digits. A building with address $a_1a_2a_3\ldots$ receives its own mail iff $a_{i+k}=a_i$ for all $i\ge1$, i.e. iff the address is $\overline{a_1a_2\cdots a_k}$ (a purely periodic address with a block of length $k$).

Therefore a building receives its own mail for some number $k$ of deleted digits exactly when its address is purely periodic, i.e. consists *solely* of a repeating block from the first digit on (equivalently, as a binary fraction it is a fraction in lowest terms with odd denominator). The buildings that never receive their own mail are exactly those whose address is **not** purely periodic: for example $1\overline{10}=1101010\ldots$ (its tail repeats, but not from the first digit) or $11010010001\ldots$ (the runs of $0$s grow).

solutions.title: Take the periodic address

A *neighborhood* $N$ of size $r>0$ around $h_1$ is the set of addresses $h$ whose distance from $h_1$ is less than $r$: $N(h_1,r)=\{h: d(h,h_1)<r\}$.

If $h=\overline{1100}$, list three elements $h_i$ of $N\!\left(h,\frac1{16}\right)$ and describe all such $h_i$ in general.

solutions.title: Agree on the first four places
solutions.body: $d(h,h_i)<\frac1{16}=2^{-4}$ means the first difference is in place $5$ or later (or there is none), i.e. $h_i$ agrees with $h=1100\ldots$ in the first four places. So $N\!\left(h,\frac1{16}\right)$ consists of all addresses $1100h'$ where $h'$ is any address. Examples: $1100\overline0$, $11001\overline0$, $110011\overline0$.

The address of the Cantor post office is $000\ldots=\overline0$.

A *neighborhood* of size $r>0$ around $h_1$ is the set $N(h_1,r)=\{h: d(h,h_1)<r\}$.

Is it possible to describe the set of all addresses at a distance of *more* than $\frac1{16}$ from the Cantor post office as a neighborhood of size $r<\frac12$ around any particular address? If so, give the address and the value of $r$. If not, demonstrate why not.

solutions.title: Look at first digits
solutions.body:
Addresses at distance more than $\frac1{16}$ from the post office $\overline0$ are those that first differ from $\overline0$ in place $1$, $2$ or $3$: distance $\frac12$ (address starts with $1$), $\frac14$ (starts $01$), $\frac18$ (starts $001$). So the set contains addresses starting with $1$ and others starting with $0$.

Suppose this set were $N(x,r)$ with $r<\frac12$. Every $h$ in it satisfies $d(h,x)<\frac12$, so $h$ cannot differ from $x$ in the first place (that would give distance $\frac12$). Hence all addresses in $N(x,r)$ have the same first digit as $x$. But the set contains addresses beginning with $0$ and addresses beginning with $1$, a contradiction. **No.** ∎

A *neighborhood* of size $r>0$ around $h_1$ is the set $N(h_1,r)=\{h: d(h,h_1)<r\}$. Use the triangle inequality $d(h_1,h_2)+d(h_2,h_3)\ge d(h_1,h_3)$ for any three addresses (Problem 2b).

Prove that if $h_1$ and $h_2$ are distinct addresses in Cantor County, then there exist neighborhoods $N(h_1,r_1)$ and $N(h_2,r_2)$ such that $N(h_1,r_1)\cap N(h_2,r_2)=\varnothing$.
answer: Take $r_1=r_2=2^{-(n+1)}$ where $n$ is the first place where $h_1,h_2$ differ.

solutions.title: Radius half the distance
solutions.body:
Suppose $h_1,h_2$ first differ in place $n$, so $d(h_1,h_2)=2^{-n}$. Let $r_1=r_2=2^{-(n+1)}$. If an address $x$ lay in both neighborhoods, then
$$d(h_1,h_2)\le d(h_1,x)+d(x,h_2)<2^{-(n+1)}+2^{-(n+1)}=2^{-n}=d(h_1,h_2),$$
a contradiction. So the two neighborhoods are disjoint. ∎

If $D\neq\varnothing$, the *distance* between $h_1$ and $h_2$, written $d(h_1,h_2)$, equals $2^{-n}$ where $n$ is the smallest element of $D$. If $D=\varnothing$, then $d(h_1,h_2)=0$. The address of the Cantor post office is $000\ldots=\overline0$.

The post office decides to use the digit $2$ as well. Each existing building is assigned a new address whose digits are chosen from $\{0,1,2\}$ instead of $\{0,1\}$. As in the old address system, a digit need not be used. However, when the post office starts assigning addresses to *new* buildings, the bureaucrats realize, to their shock, that the way in which the post office assigned new addresses to old buildings used up all the new addresses. Show that this is possible by constructing a one-to-one correspondence between the old addresses and the new addresses.
answer: A bijection exists: match the non-terminating-in-0s sequences through $(0,1]$ (binary vs ternary expansions), and the (countably many) sequences ending in $\overline0$ with each other.

solutions.title: Binary and ternary expansions of numbers in $(0,1]$
solutions.body:
Let $B$ be the set of all infinite $0$-$1$ sequences (old addresses) and $T$ the set of all infinite $0$-$1$-$2$ sequences (new addresses). Let $E_B\subset B$ be the sequences that end in an infinite string of $0$s, and $E_T\subset T$ likewise.

**Main part.** Every real number $x\in(0,1]$ has exactly one binary expansion $x=\sum a_i2^{-i}$ that does not end in all $0$s (using the expansion ending in all $1$s for dyadic numbers, e.g. $\frac12=0.0111\ldots_2$), and exactly one ternary expansion $x=\sum c_i3^{-i}$ that does not end in all $0$s. So the map $B\setminus E_B\to(0,1]$ taking a sequence to its binary value is a bijection, and so is $T\setminus E_T\to(0,1]$. Composing the first with the inverse of the second gives a bijection $\varphi:B\setminus E_B\to T\setminus E_T$: send $a_1a_2\ldots$ to the ternary digits of the number whose binary digits it is. (For example $\overline{10}=\frac23$ maps to $\frac23=0.2222\ldots_3$, i.e. to $\overline2$.)

**The leftover sequences.** $E_B$ is countably infinite: the sequences with all digits after place $n$ equal to $0$ form a finite set ($2^n$ sequences) for each $n$, and $E_B$ is the union over $n$; it is infinite. Likewise $E_T$ is countably infinite. Hence there is a bijection $\psi:E_B\to E_T$ (list the elements of each set as $e_1,e_2,\ldots$ and send $e_i\mapsto f_i$).

Putting $\varphi$ and $\psi$ together gives a bijection $B\to T$: every old address receives exactly one new address, and every new address is used exactly once. ∎
